title: The Stone Book Where Erosion Writes Chapters

features.name: the-text-that-erosion-makes
features.desc-on-touch: The stone has been read so many times by water that the words have started to show. Each groove is a sentence the limestone has been trying to say.

features.name: the-fence-of-comparison
features.desc-on-touch: Two fences run parallel through the stone, one carved by time, one by intent. They read each other across the space between. The corrosion moves both ways.

features.name: the-shelf-s-library
features.desc-on-touch: Shelves of stone, each one a closed chapter, each one still being written by the water that drips past it. The books here are thick with years.

features.name: the-current-that-reads-backwards
features.desc-on-touch: Water flows through grooves it has carved, reading its own erosions, comparing what it was to what it has made. The script it traces never repeats.

inscription: the limestone here speaks in the language that erosion teaches: each layer a sentence, each sentence rewritten by water until the stone no longer knows what it meant to say

file.name: Layer_Comparisons_Pl33_Pl34_Limestone_Profile.txt
file.note: A technical record of stone stratification. The corruption: each layer description contains a memory of what shaped it. The archive cannot distinguish between geological observation and lived time.

reverie.title: REVERIE — kneeling where stone learns to read
narr: You kneel at the limestone edge with her. She runs her finger
along the grooves that water cut. 'Each one,' she says, 'is a
year the stone tried to remember itself.' You trace the path
the river carved—not knowing, not planning, just flowing past
until the stone gave way. 'It's a kind of reading,' she whispers.
'The stone and the water, reading each other into shape.'

deeper where the stone learns to argue with itself
